title: Challenging the Myth of the 10x Programmer
channel: Software Engineering Institute | Carnegie Mellon University
summary: SEI researcher on data showing the 10x programmer range is mostly within-person variation, with implications for small tasks and sprint length.

assertions.quote: the variation within a programmer within a programmer's own 10 programs was comparable to the variation between programmers

verdicts.note: Nichols' repeated-measures PSP data support this, but the sample is trained PSP students on small exercises and other studies still find stable individual differences.

Re-analysis of 61 experiments (614 subjects) finds the slowest-quarter to fastest-quarter median ratio is typically 2-3x and max/min ratios above 10 are rare, so the 10x spread is an artifact of best-vs-worst comparison; the report does not measure a programmer's own task-to-task variation.

assertions.quote: what about degrees obtained nothing mattered

verdicts.note: This null result holds in the PSP dataset, but other studies find modest effects of relevant experience, so it is not settled.

assertions.quote: the distribution isn't a bells curve it's more log normal long tail

verdicts.note: Task-time distributions are commonly right-skewed, consistent with this, though the exact form varies by dataset.

Work time distributions across 1491 observations show a clear long right tail (skewness about 1 to 2) and a normal assumption over-estimates variability almost always; the paper confirms long-tailed non-normal shape but does not fit a log-normal.

assertions.quote: it's easier to estimate it's easier to know when it's gone off the rails

verdicts.note: Estimation error grows with task size in most estimation research; the early-intervention benefit is plausible but less directly measured.

In one three-week student XP project, initial estimates were about one third of actuals, blamed on inexperience and coarse user stories, and improved as the project went on; a single small case bearing only on the story-granularity half of the claim.

Controlled experiments show a magnitude effect: smaller tasks are overestimated or at least less underestimated while larger tasks are underestimated, so small tasks carry less bias; the early-warning benefit is not studied.

assertions.quote: what happens when you reduce your sample size the uncertainty becomes bigger

verdicts.note: Statistically sound for sprint-level forecasting, but no study pins down where the diminishing returns begin.

assertions.quote: you're going to be hard-pressed to really up the productivity by finding that super fast programmer

verdicts.note: Follows from the variance finding, but environmental interventions have not been compared head-to-head with hiring in controlled studies.
